entities.summary:
Count Ivan Andreyevich Osterman (died 1811-04-30) was a pivotal Russian statesman and diplomat whose career as Vice-Chancellor (1781–1797) and Chancellor (1797–1799) profoundly shaped Imperial Russia's foreign policy during the late 18th century. Operating at the zenith of Catherine the Great’s reign and the tumultuous early years of Paul I, Osterman inherited a legacy of diplomatic acumen from his father, Andrei Osterman, a close advisor to Peter the Great. His tenure coincided with Russia's aggressive territorial expansion and consolidation of its status as a premier European power, particularly through the partitions of Poland and engagements with the Ottoman Empire.

Osterman’s diplomatic efforts were instrumental in navigating the complex geopolitical landscape of late 18th-century Europe. As Vice-Chancellor, he directly advised Catherine II, contributing to the formulation and execution of policies that led to the Second (1793) and Third (1795) Partitions of Poland, which significantly expanded Russia's western borders. He also played a crucial role in managing relations during the Russo-Turkish War (1787–1792), which concluded with the Treaty of Jassy, solidifying Russian control over the Black Sea northern coast and the Crimea. His expertise extended to securing alliances and influencing European courts, maintaining Russia's strategic interests against rival powers like Sweden and France.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ivan Osterman was a key figure in late 18th-century Russian diplomacy, directly contributing to Russia's substantial territorial gains from the partitions of Poland and solidifying its Black Sea influence. His efforts significantly shaped Russia's imperial trajectory and its status as a major European power.
